newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch EU conference aims to tackle trade in women.
newsitem.headline: Dutch EU conference aims to tackle trade in women.

text.p: Delegates gathered in the Hague on Thursday for an international conference to promote a coordinated crackdown on trafficking in women for the European Union's booming sex industry.

After two days of closed-door discussions between interest groups, police and observers from prospective EU member states in eastern Europe, the conference will on Saturday bring in EU ministers to try to hammer out a code of conduct for member states.

Figures from the International Organization for Migration show some 500,000 women were sold for sexual exploitation in the EU in 1995, with many coming from the former East Bloc, and the European Commission recognises that the trend is on the rise.

"Thousands of women are being trafficked from developing countries and Central and Eastern Europe to Western Europe and brought into quasi-slavery," the Commission said in a recent report to the European Parliament.

"Trafficking in women for sexual exploitation is an increasing type of international organised crime generating high profits with relatively low forms of risk. Only a minority of cases are reported and convictions of traffickers are rare."
Themes to be discussed at the conference include prevention, detection and the harsher prosecution of those running the trade.

"There are large enterprises and international networks creating a sophisticated and well-organised 'industry', with political support and economic resources in countries of origin, transit and destination," the Commission said.
Proposals for an EU code of conduct to combat trafficking will be presented by the Dutch government, which has made the issue a priority of its six-month EU presidency.
A key thrust of the Dutch approach is to target traffickers, rather than victims, by ensuring exploited women living illegally in the EU can seek help without risking immediate deportation.

"The current policies in the majority of member states deter women from reporting to the authorities, as they are faced with arrest, detention and expulsion as illegal aliens and/or prostitutes," a background document says.
"Too often it is the victim who turns out to stand trial instead of the offender."
The Netherlands, which tolerates but closely monitors prostitution, grants temporary residence permits to women forced into the sex trade to allow them to testify against their captors.

Other recommendations for the code of conduct include victim compensation, prevention at source through closer contact with, and aid to, countries of origin and more effective and specialised policing.
